name: Micro-grafting FUE

lead: Micro-grafting FUE refers to hair transplantation with small grafts (usually one to a few hairs) that are extracted individually from the back of the scalp and placed in thinning areas. Small grafts are used especially at the hairline, where a soft, natural-looking edge matters.

The approach helps looks by restoring hair on the front and top of the head, framing the face and reducing the appearance of balding. Transplanted follicles keep the growth traits of the donor area, which is why the result is long-lasting, and the technique has been described in the medical literature for decades.

paras: A surgeon extracts follicular units from the donor area with small punches under local anaesthesia and places them in the recipient area, with single-hair grafts at the front and larger units behind. Recovery after FUE is typically under a week, and new growth appears over many months. Many people also use medical hair loss treatments alongside surgery.

Temporary thinning of transplanted hair (shock loss) is common. Other risks include infection, scarring in the donor area, uneven density, and the cost and long surgical time. Outcomes depend on donor supply and surgeon skill, and ongoing hair loss can change the overall pattern.

angle.text: Small grafts rebuild the hairline and thin areas with hair that grows from the donor site. Using one-hair grafts in front is intended to mimic natural hair, which is why people interested in hairline restoration discuss the technique.

lead: Micro-grafting FUE is a hair transplant approach that combines follicular unit extraction (FUE) with small grafts. In FUE, individual follicular units of one to four hairs are removed with punches of roughly 0.6 to 1.0 mm under local anaesthesia, leaving small punctate scars and requiring no stitch removal, with recovery of under a week [1].

Micrografts are the small grafts that replaced the old doll-hair look of large plugs. A French plastic surgery review noted that the typical tufted effect of old macrografts disappeared with the shift to micrografts [2], and a dermatology review described follicular units, groups of one to three hairs emerging from a single orifice, as a fundamental technical advance that gives permanent hair restoration in male and female baldness [3].

Permanence rests on a principle established by dermatologist Norman Orentreich in the late 1950s: transplanted grafts are donor dominant and keep the growth characteristics of their original site [1]. In looksmaxxing circles the technique is discussed mainly for hairline design, where single-hair grafts create a natural edge.

paras: Hair grows in natural groups of one to four hairs, and transplanting these units in their natural groupings supports a natural look [1]. In FUE, units are taken one at a time rather than dissected from a strip, which leaves small punctate scars instead of a linear one. Wikipedia notes FUE takes longer and costs more than strip harvesting, and that some surgeons report a lower ratio of successfully transplanted follicles [1].
Micrografts refers to the small grafts themselves. Surgeons place the smallest grafts at the front of the hairline and use larger units behind for density.

Orentreich showed in the late 1950s that grafts are donor dominant [1]. In the late 1980s Limmer introduced the stereo microscope to dissect donor strips into micrografts [1]. A 2003 review describes baldness surgery as redistribution from hair-rich to hair-poor areas, and notes that micrografts removed the tufted effect of earlier large grafts [2]. A 2002 review described follicular units as simple and painless permanent restoration [3].

Temporary hair thinning, or shock loss, is common after transplantation [1]. Wikipedia also lists infection risk, with antibiotics often prescribed, and notes that alcohol and smoking can impair graft survival [1]. FUE also has a demanding learning curve for surgeons [1].
The cited sources are narrative reviews of baldness surgery and micrograft indications that describe the technique and its place in hair restoration [2][3].

timeline.event: Orentreich shows that transplanted grafts are donor dominant [1].
Limmer introduces the stereo microscope for micrograft dissection [1].
French review describes follicular unit micrografts as a fundamental technical progress [3].
